newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-BUSINESSMAN ADMITS HE GOT ADVICE FROM SOCCER STARS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BUSINESSMAN ADMITS HE GOT ADVICE FROM SOCCER STARS.

text.p: A Malaysian
businessman on trial for match fixing admitted on Monday he had
received inside information from top soccer stars which he then
passed on to a Far Eastern betting syndicate.
Heng Suan Lim told a court that players such as former
Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar and Hans Segers had given
him tips which he used to advise the syndicate which matches to
bet on in Malaysia and Indonesia.
"They wouldn't have that information (there). It's extremely
useful," he said, adding that he also obtained some information
from newspapers and television.
Grobbelaar, Segers, and striker John Fashanu face charges
along with Lim, 31, of conspiring to fix English premier league
matches. They deny the charges.
They are accused of conspiring together to give and accept
gifts of money as inducements to influence the outcome of soccer
matches improperly or as rewards for having done so.
If convicted, they could face sentences of up to seven years
in jail and unlimited fines.
Asked by his lawyer Jerome Lynch what other sources he had
used, Lim replied: "Soccer players, after I got to know them --
Fashanu, Segers, Grobbelaar."
He said former Wimbledon striker Roger Joseph and current
Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich had also provided some
information.
The prosecution says Lim is the so-called "short man" who
helped pay Grobbelaar and Segers for rigging matches. Lim
received more than 500,000 pounds ($800,000) from Far Eastern
sources including more than 100,000 pounds from Indonesian
businessman Johannes Josef.
Lim said Josef was a close friend of his mother's who had
originally sent him money while he (Lim) studied accountancy in
London but later offered to pay for hints on the outcome of
future English soccer matches.
"He said, You can give me information, because quality
information is very difficult to get (in Indonesia)'."
